arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Ortiz argued the case asks whether the felon-in-possession statute prevents courts from ordering the transfer of seized firearms to a third party.
Justice Kennedy asked if a black-letter case supports the proposition that courts have general equitable authority to order such transfers.
Justice Kennedy asked under what statutory rule or authority the court holds the hearing on the transfer.
Justice Sotomayor asked if the side that brought the case was on a futile mission in this circuit regarding the transfer request.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the scope of federal court authority over seized property. the side that brought the case seeks a court order to transfer his guns to a third party. The government argues the statute bars such orders. The core legal question is whether the felon-in-possession statute prevents courts from directing the transfer of seized firearms.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Court to allow the transfer of his seized guns to a third party.
The government wants the Court to uphold the ban on transferring the guns to a third party.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues the felon-in-possession statute does not prevent courts from ordering the transfer of seized firearms to a suitable third party.
The government argues the statute prohibits courts from ordering the transfer of a felon's seized firearms to a third party.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the limits of federal court power over seized property. It determines whether courts can direct the transfer of a felon's guns to third parties. The outcome shapes how courts handle seized firearms in criminal cases. It affects the balance between property rights and public safety.
